headline: NurGaz paid 10.9bn som to the budget, a third of 2026 revenue as 2027 draft nears
dek: Royalties and profit tax from one company outweigh every other source of ISEZ income, and only a summary of the budget is ever published.
paragraphs: NurGaz paid 10.9 billion som in royalties and profit tax into the budget of the Irad Special Economic Zone in 2025, equal to about a third of the 32.4 billion som the ISEZ expects to collect in 2026, according to the company's own annual report. No other single source brings in as much.

The figures come from NurGaz's Annual Report 2025, an abridged notice printed as a paid advertisement in Vecherniy Nurzhan on 3 July and signed by the company's president, K. Bekzatov, and its chief accountant, L. Ivashchenko. It states royalties of US$842.3 million and profit tax of US$455.8 million, together US$1,298.1 million. At the official rate of 8.40 som to the dollar, that is 10,904 million som.

The same notice puts NurGaz's 2025 revenue at US$2,640.4 million and net profit at US$312 million. Taxes and royalties to the budget therefore equalled roughly half of the company's turnover, and about four times its profit. Output reached 92,000 barrels a day, the highest since 1991, from 4,581 thousand tonnes of crude.

The Ministry of Economy, under Minister Dinara Usupova, drafts the ISEZ budget. The Governor's office sends it to the Mejlis in November and it passes in December. The 2026 budget summary set revenue at 32.4 billion som against spending of 34.9 billion, with the 2.5 billion deficit covered from the Toktogul export escrow reserve at Talasbank. It put NurGaz royalties and profit tax at about 36 per cent of revenue, a little above the share the 2025 payments imply; the two figures cover different years.

Asked whether the 2027 draft would be published in full, the Ministry's press secretary, Bekbolot Sherov, said: "Only a summary of the budget is published, as in every year. The Mejlis receives the full draft." He did not say how much of 2027 revenue the draft expects from NurGaz.

Prof. Raisa Akmatova, an economist at Talas State University, said the concentration was the central fact of the budget. "When one company carries a third of revenue, the state's spending is in effect an oil forecast," she said. "A bad year for crude, or a dispute over the pipeline, would reach teachers' pay and pensions within months." She noted that public wages take about 34 per cent of spending, and that the escrow reserve already covers the gap.

Prof. Sergei Volkov, a petroleum engineer at the Nurzhan Polytechnic Institute, said the 2025 output record owed much to water-flooding of the older Chu blocks and 46 new wells, which the report says were drilled with Chevron. "Water-flooding holds output up; it does not raise it for ever," he said. Output, he added, was the part of the picture the company reports in detail.

The company does not publish full audited accounts. The abridged notice gives payments, profit, staff (14,920) and investment (US$318 million), but not the cost lines or the contracts behind them, and the budget summary does not break down its NurGaz line. NurGaz did not reply to questions from the Herald by deadline.

The antimony combine's payments, with customs and transit duties, make up a smaller part of the revenue the Ministry counts. The draft is due before the Mejlis before the end of the month. Deputies will vote on it in December, on a summary the public will also see.
